name: Artificial tears

card.summary: Over-the-counter lubricating eye drops for dry, irritated eyes: standard first-line comfort care, not a whitening or redness fix.
card.aka: Lubricant eye drops, eye lubricants, rewetting drops
card.note: Redness-relief drops containing vasoconstrictors such as tetrahydrozoline are a different product class; a 2023 contamination recall of some brands was linked to serious infections.

quick.overview:
Artificial tears are lubricating eye drops, gels and ointments sold mostly without prescription. They are used for dry eye and for irritation from screens, wind, contact lenses or surgery, and in appearance circles they are discussed as a way to keep the eye surface comfortable and less irritated-looking.

They come with or without preservatives, in thin liquid or thicker gel forms. Reviews and guidance describe them as the usual first step for dry eye, though no single formulation has been shown to be best.
quick.mechanism: They supplement and stabilise the tear film that coats the eye, using water, salts and thickening polymers such as carboxymethylcellulose, hypromellose or hyaluronic acid. They do not contain the living components of natural tears and do not treat the underlying cause of dryness.
quick.risks: Temporary blurred vision is the most common effect, especially with gels and ointments. Preservatives such as benzalkonium chloride can irritate the eye surface with frequent use, which is why preservative-free vials are recommended for heavy use. In 2023 a recall of certain brands followed bacterial contamination linked to eye infections, vision loss and a death. Drops marketed to remove redness contain different active ingredients.

lead: Artificial tears are lubricating eye drops, gels and ointments that are designed to relieve dryness and irritation of the ocular surface. They are sold mostly over the counter and are used mainly for dry eye disease, for contact lens comfort and during or after some eye procedures [2][4].

Formulations are built from water, electrolytes and thickening polymers such as carboxymethylcellulose, polyvinyl alcohol, hypromellose, hydroxypropyl cellulose or hyaluronic acid. They are made with or without preservatives, and as thin drops for daytime or thicker gels and ointments for longer-lasting but vision-blurring effect [2][1].

Published reviews have found no clear single best formulation, and many trials of individual products are small or open-label [2]. In looksmaxxing and appearance contexts artificial tears are sometimes discussed as supportive eye-surface care, distinct from whitening drops or surgical options.
infobox: Carboxymethylcellulose, hypromellose, polyvinyl alcohol, hyaluronic acid, electrolytes

paras: Dry eye is the most common indication. Risk factors listed in encyclopedic summaries include older age, female sex, dry environments, certain medications, autoimmune disease such as Sjogren syndrome, contact lens wear and some eye surgeries [2][1].

Artificial tears are also used to rewet contact lenses, to lubricate the eye during examinations, and in hospital eye care for people who cannot blink fully, such as some critically ill patients [4][3].

Dry or irritated eyes can look red or tired, and appearance-focused communities sometimes mention lubricating drops as a comfort measure. The evidence base concerns dryness symptoms and tear-film measures, not eye whiteness or other cosmetic outcomes.

Preserved products in multi-dose bottles are common and inexpensive. Preservative-free single-use vials are recommended in encyclopedic summaries for people who react to preservatives or who need drops many times a day [2][1]. Gels and ointments are thicker and longer-lasting but can temporarily blur vision [2].

Some formulations add lipids to target evaporative dry eye, and others use hypotonic solutions for aqueous-deficient dry eye [1]. A related category, autologous serum drops made from a patient's own blood, is used for ocular surface disease under clinical supervision and has been reviewed separately [5].

Temporary blurred vision is the most frequently reported effect. Allergic reactions to ingredients are possible [2]. High concentrations of the preservative benzalkonium chloride have been reported to damage the corneal surface and reduce tear and mucin production, which is why preservative-free options are advised with frequent use [2].

In February 2023 a manufacturer recalled artificial tears sold under the EzriCare and Delsam Pharma names after a multi-state cluster of drug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections was linked to them, including cases of permanent vision loss and one death [2].

Products sold to remove redness that contain vasoconstrictors such as tetrahydrozoline are sometimes mistaken for lubricants. Encyclopedic sources note that prolonged use can cause desensitisation to the drug [2].

Trials of artificial tears are numerous but mostly small and product-specific. An open-label evaluation of a hydroxypropyl-guar gellable lubricant in adults with moderate dry eye assessed signs and symptoms of dryness [6]. Research on tear dynamics has found that tear turnover is reduced in people with symptomatic dry eye, one of the physiological rationales for tear supplementation [7].

Registered studies include small trials of tear osmolarity with sustained use of a branded lubricant [8][9], a trial of two lubricant drops in dry eye disease [10], and a trial of lubricating drops after cataract surgery [11]. A Cochrane review summarised in an encyclopedic source found no clearly superior formulation [2].

A meta-analysis of randomised trials compared moisture chambers with lubrication for corneal protection in intensive care patients and noted limited evidence for choosing between them [3]. No published trials were identified that test artificial tears for cosmetic whitening or appearance outcomes.

Eye remedies for dryness are described in ancient Egyptian medical texts, according to one encyclopedic account, and saline solutions and later polymer- and lipid-based products followed in the 19th and 20th centuries [1].
